behavior_items: The reproducer defines a named C++23 module `Coll` that imports `std` and exports a class `Coll` whose only data member is `std::vector<int> vals;`. This means the layout, constructor, destructor, and special member semantics of `Coll` depend directly on the standard library vector implementation made visible through the imported `std` module.

The exported factory `createColl()` returns `Coll{}` by value. Constructing that prvalue requires default construction of the embedded `std::vector<int>`. In the caller, storing the return value in `auto coll = createColl();` also guarantees that `coll` must later be destroyed at end of `main`, so the generated code must be able to emit or reference the complete destructor chain for `Coll` and then for `std::vector<int>`.

`Coll` does not declare any special members, so its destructor is implicitly declared and implicitly defined by the compiler. Because `Coll` contains a `std::vector<int>`, the synthesized destructor for `Coll` is required to invoke `std::vector<int>::~vector()`, which in turn destroys its internal `_Vector_base<int, allocator<int>>::_Vector_impl` state. The undefined symbol named in the linker error is exactly the destructor of that implementation subobject: `_ZNSt12_Vector_baseIiSaIiEE12_Vector_implD1Ev`.

The important aspect of the test is that the importing translation unit (`testcoll.cpp`) never names `std::vector<int>` directly. It only uses the exported class `Coll` indirectly, through module interface metadata. This exercises GCC's handling of transitive module dependencies: after importing `Coll`, the consumer must still have enough semantic and code generation information to instantiate or reference every required standard library special member used by `Coll`'s implicit destructor.

The bug report title highlights this as an 'indirect use of an exported class using a vector'. That is precisely the path being tested: a standard library template specialization is embedded in an exported class, then used only via another module import. If the same vector were used directly in the consumer, or if `Coll` had an explicitly out-of-line destructor emitted in the module unit, the failure mode could differ. The reproducer isolates the transitive, implicit-special-member case.

The command line builds the standard library module interface separately using `-fmodule-only -c bits/std.cc`, then compiles the module interface unit `collmod.cppm` and the importer `testcoll.cpp` together with `-fmodules -fsearch-include-path`. This setup stresses GCC's module BMI/object emission split: `std` is available primarily as a module artifact, not as ordinary textual headers in each translation unit, so any missing destructor emission or import linkage becomes visible at link time.

The failure occurs at link stage rather than during parsing or template instantiation. That means GCC successfully accepts the declarations, understands the class layout, and generates object code references, but fails to ensure that a definition of the needed vector implementation destructor is emitted into any object file or resolved from the standard module build artifacts. In other words, this is not a front-end syntax or type-checking bug; it is a code generation / module emission / linkage bug.

The undefined symbol specifically points at a non-inline or non-emitted standard library implementation detail that should have been available when the implicitly generated destructor path was materialized. GCC appears to generate a call from the importer-side destruction of `Coll`, but the corresponding standard library destructor body for the vector internals is not instantiated or emitted into a linked object in this module configuration.

Because `createColl()` returns an empty `Coll`, runtime behavior would be trivial if linking succeeded: the vector would be default-initialized empty, no allocations would occur, and destruction would just tear down an empty vector state. The reproducer therefore proves the bug is independent of dynamic allocation or element management; merely requiring the destructor path of a `std::vector<int>` member is enough to trigger the missing symbol.

This is a good minimal module reproducer because it removes unrelated complexity: no user-defined destructor, no mutation of the vector, no templates in user code, no cross-module inheritance, and no exceptions. The only essential ingredients are an exported class, a standard library member type coming from `import std;`, a returned object whose lifetime ends in an importing translation unit, and thus an implicitly generated destructor that crosses the module boundary.

Semantically, the importer should not need to know private implementation details of `std::vector<int>` such as `_Vector_impl`; those details are an ABI concern hidden behind the standard library interface. The fact that the linker error exposes `_Vector_implD1Ev` shows GCC/libstdc++ module handling leaked an internal dependency that was not fully materialized for linkage when the type was consumed indirectly through another module.

Overall, the reproducer exercises GCC's treatment of exported class definitions containing standard library template members, propagation of implicit special member requirements through module interfaces, and emission/linkage of standard library destructor code when `std` is consumed as a named module rather than through textual inclusion.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer tests a transitive C++ modules case where module `Coll` exports a class containing `std::vector<int>`, and another translation unit imports `Coll` and simply creates a returned object. That is enough to require GCC to synthesize and link the implicit destructor of `Coll`, which must destroy the embedded `std::vector<int>`. GCC accepts the program, but at link time the generated destruction path references the internal libstdc++ symbol for `_Vector_impl`'s destructor and no definition is provided. So the bug is a module-related code generation/linkage failure: indirect use of an exported class with a `std::vector` member does not pull in or emit all needed standard library destructor definitions when `std` is built/imported as a module.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: Common pattern: the failure is triggered only when a standard library template specialization (`std::vector<int>`) is used indirectly through an exported class in a named module, and the consuming translation unit never names the vector type directly. GCC successfully parses and type-checks the program, synthesizes the implicit destructor for the exported class, and emits code that references the vector destruction path, but link-time resolution fails for an internal libstdc++ destructor symbol. That combination strongly points away from a user-code semantic bug and toward a compiler/modules defect in propagating or materializing implicit special-member and template-instantiation requirements across module boundaries. The key step is importer-side destruction of `Coll`: GCC appears to know that `Coll::~Coll()` must destroy `std::vector<int>`, yet it does not ensure that the needed destructor definition for the imported standard-library specialization is emitted in some object file or made reachable from the separately built `std` module artifacts. This pattern is especially consistent with a bug in module BMI serialization/deserialization of implicit special members, deferred template instantiation/emission for imported entities, or wrong ownership/linkage assignment for inline/template destructor bodies when `import std` is used instead of textual inclusion.
possible_causes: GCC modules front end may fail to serialize or reconstruct the full implicit-destructor dependency graph for an exported class with a non-trivial imported member, so the importer generates a call/reference to `std::vector<int>` destruction without triggering emission of the required libstdc++ specialization code.

Template instantiation ownership across module boundaries may be assigned to the wrong translation unit: the `std::vector<int>` destructor or one of its internal base/member destructors is treated as already provided by the `std` module BMI, while the `std` module object built with `-fmodule-only` does not actually emit the needed definition.

Code generation for imported standard-library inline/template special members may incorrectly suppress COMDAT/weak emission in the consumer when the type is reached only transitively through an exported class, causing a reference to `_Vector_implD1Ev` with no TU taking responsibility for defining it.

The importer-side synthesis of `Coll`'s implicit destructor may use incomplete or stale module metadata for `std::vector<int>` special members, leading GCC to emit an external call to an ABI-internal destructor symbol instead of instantiating/expanding the correct inline destruction sequence.

There may be a bug in how GCC handles `import std` built as a named module with `-fmodule-only`: declarations are made visible for semantic analysis, but required object-code emission for template/special-member definitions from libstdc++ is not coupled correctly to later consuming TUs.

Module dependency propagation may be incomplete for transitive non-exported implementation requirements: importing `Coll` gives enough type information for layout and overload resolution, but not enough linkage/emission information for hidden standard-library implementation members needed by implicit destruction.
evidence: The undefined symbol is `_ZNSt12_Vector_baseIiSaIiEE12_Vector_implD1Ev`, which is part of the destructor chain of `std::vector<int>` and matches the only non-trivial member of exported class `Coll`.

`Coll` declares no destructor, so GCC must synthesize `Coll::~Coll()` implicitly; that destructor necessarily destroys `std::vector<int> vals`, making the failure about implicit special-member generation/emission rather than explicit user code.

The consumer TU only does `auto coll = createColl();` and never names `std::vector<int>` directly, so the failing path is specifically transitive use of imported type information through module metadata.
Compilation succeeds and the failure appears only at link time, showing semantic analysis worked but some required definition was never emitted or made link-visible.

The `std` module is built separately with `-fmodule-only -c bits/std.cc`, which stresses GCC's split between module interface availability and object-code emission; this is consistent with missing instantiation/emission ownership for imported library entities.

The object file reporting the undefined reference is from `testcoll.cpp`, indicating the importer side generated the destructor reference for the returned `Coll` object but no linked object provided the target definition.

selected_files.reason: Most directly implicated: the failure depends on transitive C++20 module import state (`import std;` inside an exported module, then indirect use from another importer). This file owns C++ module entity import/export, CMI serialization, and reconstruction of imported declarations, making it the likeliest place for lost implicit-destructor or template-emission requirements.

`std::vector<int>` destructor code is template-based and the undefined symbol suggests the needed specialization/body was not instantiated or emitted when reached only indirectly through an exported class. This file handles template instantiation and deferred instantiation, which matches the missing transitive-instantiation pattern.

The reproducer hinges on implicit generation/emission of special members and on deciding what C++ entities are written out for linkage. This file contains C++ declaration/output logic including constructor/destructor support, so it is a strong candidate for wrong ownership or suppression of the needed destructor emission.

`Coll` has an implicitly generated destructor whose body must destroy the imported `std::vector<int>` member. If GCC synthesizes that destructor incorrectly for a module-imported member type, or fails to trigger the right subobject destruction semantics, this is a plausible source file.

A likely failure mode is that module/BMI streaming omits some tree-level dependency needed to reconstruct or emit the vector destructor path in the importing TU. This file is central to serializing trees and declarations out of module state.

Complementary to streaming out: the importer may deserialize incomplete metadata for the imported class/member destructor chain, causing later codegen to reference an external ABI symbol without arranging a definition. This file is therefore highly relevant.

The bug manifests at link time after successful semantic analysis, which suggests a missed finalization/reachability/emission decision for an implicitly needed function or variable. This file drives compilation-unit finalization and symbol discovery, so it could incorrectly skip the required destructor-related emission.

If the destructor symbol or related imported entities are assigned the wrong visibility/ownership when coming from a module import, the symbol table can end up with a reference but no defining emission. This file is a plausible lower-level contributor to that outcome.

Add NODE to queue starting at QUEUED_NODES. The queue is linked via AUX pointers and terminated by pointer to 1.

Process CGRAPH_NEW_FUNCTIONS and perform actions necessary to add these functions into callgraph in a way so they look like ordinary reachable functions inserted into callgraph already at construction time.

As an GCC extension we allow redefinition of the function. The semantics when both copies of bodies differ is not well defined. We replace the old body with new body so in unit at a time mode we always use new body, while in normal mode we may end up with old body inlined into some functions and new body expanded and inlined in others. ??? It may make more sense to use one body for inlining and other body for expanding the function but this is difficult to do. This is also used to cancel C++ mangling aliases, which can be for functions or variables.
Return true when there are references to the node. INCLUDE_SELF is true if a self reference counts as a reference.

DECL has been parsed. Take it, queue it, compile it at the whim of the logic in effect. If NO_COLLECT is true, then our caller cannot stand to have the garbage collector run at the moment. We would need to either create a new GC context, or just not compile right now.

Add the function FNDECL to the call graph. Unlike finalize_function, this function is intended to be used by middle end and allows insertion of new function at arbitrary point of compilation. The function can be either in high, low or SSA form GIMPLE. The function is assumed to be reachable and have address taken (so no API breaking optimizations are performed on it). Main work done by this function is to enqueue the function for later processing to avoid need the passes to be re-entrant.
Analyze the function scheduled to be output.

C++ frontend produce same body aliases all over the place, even before PCH gets streamed out. It relies on us linking the aliases with their function in order to do the fixups, but ipa-ref is not PCH safe. Consequently we first produce aliases without links, but once C++ FE is sure he won't stream PCH we build the links via this function.
Process a symver attribute.
Process attributes common for vars and functions.

Look for externally_visible and used attributes and mark cgraph nodes accordingly. We cannot mark the nodes at the point the attributes are processed (in handle_*_attribute) because the copy of the declarations available at that point may not be canonical. For example, in: void f(); void f() __attribute__((used)); the declaration we see in handle_used_attribute will be the second declaration -- but the front end will subsequently merge that declaration with the original declaration and discard the second declaration. Furthermore, we can't mark these nodes in finalize_function because: void f() {} void f() __attribute__((externally_visible)); is valid. So, we walk the nodes at the end of the translation unit, applying the attributes at that point.
Mark DECL as finalized. By finalizing the declaration, frontend instruct the middle end to output the variable to asm file, if needed or externally visible.
